reasons: The file is a retained prototype, and no test is visible.

terms.meaning: an instruction that sends the browser to a different address automatically
the set of rules that controls how a page looks
an early working model, kept for reference rather than maintained
the extra text after a question mark in a web address

depends_on: public/tools/lessons-learnt (the target of the redirect written as ../tools/lessons-learnt)

sections.name: File setup (part 1)
sections.title: Redirect and base page styles
sections.what: Sends visitors to the maintained lessons-learnt tool straight away, keeping any query string. Below that, it sets the color, font, and spacing values used across the page, and the basic layout of the sidebar and main area.
sections.why: Stated in the code: the comment says this is retained prototype source and old bookmarks now use the maintained tool.
sections.watch_out: The redirect runs before anything else, so the rest of this page is never shown until the redirect is removed.

sections.name: File setup (part 2)
sections.title: Sidebar, buttons, and status tags
sections.what: Styles the left navigation sidebar, the primary and ghost buttons, the selectable chips, and the colored status tags for on track, delayed, and over budget.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The status colors depend on the exact class names on-track, delayed, and over-budget, so a renamed class loses its color.

sections.name: File setup (part 3)
sections.title: View switch, admin lock, and progress strip
sections.what: Styles the HTML and PPTX view switch, the Analyst and Admin role switch, a full-screen admin lock card, an agent status banner, admin log and gate tables, the progress strip for users, and form fields for user choices.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The admin lock is only styling. Hiding it with styles does not restrict access, and the real check is not visible in these lines.

sections.name: File setup (part 4)
sections.title: Top bar, cards, and home page
sections.what: Styles the input fields for user choices, the workflow state chips, the sticky top bar, the card look, the home page hero, the statistics strip, the industry tiles, and the call-to-action band.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The right-hand panel is fixed 90 pixels from the top, so a taller top bar can overlap it.

sections.name: File setup (part 5)
sections.title: Filters, tabs, metrics, and project cards
sections.what: Styles the filter chip row, the tabs, the snapshot metric tiles with their bar charts, the lesson list, and the project cards with their add button.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Metric values turn green or red only through the pos and neg classes, so a value given neither class shows in plain ink.

sections.name: File setup (part 6)
sections.title: Company panel, project page, and timeline
sections.what: Styles the expandable company list in the right-hand panel, the project page layout with its key-value rows, overview text, lesson blocks, a stage timeline, and related project links.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The project list under each company stays hidden unless that company's open class is set.

sections.name: File setup (part 7)
sections.title: Deck preview and slide editor layout
sections.what: Styles the PowerPoint-style preview strip with its thumbnails and large stage, the three-column deck editor, slide thumbnails, the slide canvas, and the base look of a slide.
sections.why: Likely reason: thumbnails are scaled-down copies of the full slide, which is why the slide size is fixed at 960 by 540 pixels.
sections.watch_out: Thumbnails are scaled by fixed factors such as 0.146, so changing the slide size breaks the thumbnail look unless these numbers change too.

sections.name: File setup (part 8)
sections.title: House slide templates
sections.what: Styles the house slide designs: cover, agenda, chevron recipe columns, pillar columns, a two-column executive summary, and tables.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: House colors are set as variables on the house class, so a slide without that class falls back to other colors.

sections.name: File setup (part 9)
sections.title: Slide details, chat panel, and reading view
sections.what: Styles slide metrics, bullets, and notes, the floating canvas toolbar and pill buttons, the AI chat panel with its messages and input, the reading view for deck text, and the empty-state message.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: Chat messages are styled by the sender classes a and u, so a message without one of these classes loses its layout.

sections.name: File setup (part 10)
sections.title: Expert page and notice styling
sections.what: Sets the look of the Talk To An Expert page: a side panel with a dark disclaimer box, filter controls, a grid of expert cards, a search bar, and a connect button. It also styles the short pop-up notices that appear at the bottom of the screen.
sections.why: Likely reason: the expert page has its own layout, separate from the deck and industry pages, so it needs its own styles.
sections.watch_out: The side panel collapses to zero width through a CSS class, so any new content placed in that panel must still fit when it is collapsed.

sections.name: File setup (part 11)
sections.title: Keyboard focus, motion and filter styles
sections.what: Adds a visible outline when a control is selected with the keyboard, turns off most animations for users who ask their device to reduce motion, and changes the layout for screens narrower than about 1180 pixels. It also styles the filter panel, including its input grid, natural-language box, chips and preview text.
sections.why: Likely reason: keyboard and motion accessibility support, plus fitting smaller screens.
sections.watch_out: The reduced-motion rule shortens every animation on the page, so a new feature that relies on an animation finishing may appear to jump instead.

sections.name: File setup (part 12)
sections.title: Page skeleton and admin password box
sections.what: Lays out the main structure of the app: the left sidebar with the industry list and the deck button, the home page with its headline and stats, and empty containers that the script fills in for each page. It also contains a password box for the admin area.
sections.why: Likely reason: one page switches between views by showing one section at a time, so the layout is written once and filled by code.
sections.watch_out: The admin password is written in plain text in the page, so anyone who opens the page source can read it. This box does not provide real protection.

sections.name: File setup (part 13)
sections.title: Industry data setup and lookups
sections.what: Declares the industry names, taglines and colors used across the app, plus empty containers that will hold the industry, project and company data loaded from the server. It also builds lookup tables so a project or company can be found by its ID.
sections.why: The code states that data comes only from the Yard system, so the containers start empty and fill after loading. The reason for the fixed color list is not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The color dot table DOTS is declared empty here and is not filled in these lines, so color dots may stay blank unless it is set elsewhere. The lookup tables must be rebuilt whenever the industry data changes.

sections.name: File setup (part 14)
sections.title: Central app memory and version flags
sections.what: Holds the app's working memory: the open page, selected industry and project, the deck selection, filter settings, theme choices, and the status of the generation run. It also sets switches that turn off the older agent path and turn on the recipe harness route, and provides a helper that builds the agent address.
sections.why: The code states that Volume 2 generation uses the recipe harness and not the older agent, and the flags record that choice in one place.
sections.watch_out: Several keys are listed twice, such as the slide model and PPTX viewer entries. This is harmless in JavaScript but suggests copied code, and the agent address helper is inactive while the flag is on.

sections.name: File setup (part 15)
sections.title: Remembering the last generation run
sections.what: Saves the current generation run identifier in the browser so the page can pick it up after a reload. It can also ask the server for recent runs and choose one to reopen, preferring runs that are still running or that finished with output. Adding the new=1 setting in the address clears the saved run and starts fresh.
sections.why: The code suggests the goal is to let a crashed run resume from saved checkpoints, but the full reason is not stated.
sections.watch_out: This restore returns immediately while the agent flag is on, so it currently does nothing. If the flag is turned off, the run it picks may not be the one the analyst expects.

sections.name: File setup (part 16)
sections.title: Agent status, English enhancer and themes
sections.what: Checks whether the agent is available and reports its status. It also provides the English enhancement action, which is blocked while the agent is off and shows a notice instead. It holds the built-in fallback theme list and hides one theme from analysts.
sections.why: The code states the agent is switched off in Volume 2, so these actions show a message rather than calling the server.
sections.watch_out: The enhancer result message gives a hint about checking a key for any result that is not the LLM status, so the analyst should read the wording rather than assume success from the notice alone.

sections.name: File setup (part 17)
sections.title: Applying theme and custom colors
sections.what: Takes a set of colors and lets the analyst's own chosen colors override the theme's accent, navy, ink, wash and other shades. It then paints them onto the page and the slide previews, and recolors existing recipe slides so they match.
sections.why: The code recolors existing slides so previews match the colors the analyst chose.
sections.watch_out: Only values written as six hex digits are accepted, and any other input is ignored without a message.

sections.name: File setup (part 18)
sections.title: Per-slide color choices
sections.what: Helper functions do the color arithmetic, such as mixing a color with white to make a lighter tint, and pick a color scheme for each slide type. For example, cover slides get a navy banner, pillar slides cycle through several colors, and case profiles turn green or red based on their outcome.
sections.why: Likely reason: makes different kinds of slides easy to tell apart at a glance.
sections.watch_out: Slide types are matched by name. A new slide type not in the list falls back to an alternating accent and navy scheme with no warning.

sections.name: File setup (part 19)
sections.title: Fonts, saved colors and theme package
sections.what: Adds a Google font link when a font is chosen, sets the slide font for the page, reads the color boxes the analyst filled in, and saves them in the browser. It also builds the theme settings package that is sent to the server when a deck is made.
sections.why: The code saves choices in browser storage so they survive a reload. The reason for loading the font from Google is visible from how it is used.
sections.watch_out: Loading a Google font needs internet access; without it the slide font quietly falls back to Calibri. The theme package uses 'house' as its fallback default while the rest of the app uses 'megaprojects'.

sections.name: File setup (part 20)
sections.title: Loading and changing the theme
sections.what: On startup, loads the saved theme and custom colors from the browser and applies them, using only the built-in fallback themes in Volume 2. When the analyst picks another theme, it saves the choice, recolors the page, refreshes the deck view and shows a short notice.
sections.why: The code states Volume 2 never fetches themes from the agent, so the theme list is built in.
sections.watch_out: The starting theme depends on a URL setting, the saved value, or a fallback. The fallback name differs between the normal path and the error path, so check which one applies if the wrong theme appears.

sections.name: File setup (part 21)
sections.title: Shared helpers and project date checks
sections.what: Gives the app short helper functions: a selector for finding page elements, a function that makes text safe to show on the page, and labels and checks for each project. The checks work out a project's year from its start or end date and decide whether it counts as completed, based on lifecycle words or its end year.
sections.why: The escape helper exists so text from the data is shown as text rather than read as page code.
sections.watch_out: The escape helper does not change double quotes, so text placed inside an attribute value could break the page. The project year is read only from the first four characters of a date.

sections.name: File setup (part 22)
sections.title: Project filter matching rules
sections.what: Decides whether one project passes the current filters: status, geography, sector, age in years, completed-only evidence, and search words. A sector filter that only repeats the industry name is ignored. A plain-English prompt with no structured filters shows no projects until it has been interpreted.
sections.why: The comment says the empty result for an uninterpreted prompt is intentional, so an unclear request does not show the whole list by mistake.
sections.watch_out: Because an uninterpreted prompt gives zero projects, a phrasing the parser misses looks like an empty result rather than an error.

sections.name: File setup (part 23)
sections.title: Finding the active industry and projects
sections.what: Works out which industry is selected by reading the dropdown text, the saved choice, or the first industry in the list. It returns that industry's projects, the projects that pass the filters, whether any filter is on, and the count.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. The lists are recalculated each time so they stay in step with the filter box.
sections.watch_out: Industry matching uses partial text, so a loose name can select the wrong industry. If nothing matches, the first industry in the list is used with no notice.

sections.name: File setup (part 24)
sections.title: Filter labels and prompt parsing start
sections.what: Builds the summary line that shows how many projects match and how many will be assessed, plus the chips that list active filters. It also begins reading a plain-English request, picking out time windows such as last five years, completed-only evidence, and status words such as over budget or delayed.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets an analyst type a request in plain English and see it turned into filters without calling an outside service.
sections.watch_out: When no number is set, the summary falls back to a fixed count of 136, which could show a misleading total.

sections.name: File setup (part 25)
sections.title: Geography and sector detection from text
sections.what: Finishes reading the plain-English request. It looks for phrases such as in USA or from Chile, or a bare country name, to set geography. It then matches sector keywords such as lithium or nuclear, can switch to the matching industry, and keeps leftover words as a search term.
sections.why: Likely reason: the simple text reading runs first and cheaply, so the server reading is needed only when this finds nothing.
sections.watch_out: These are simple word patterns. Lithium is checked before mining, so mixed requests are resolved by that order, and unknown words become search text rather than being understood.

sections.name: File setup (part 26)
sections.title: Country names and geography matching
sections.what: Standardizes country spellings such as USA variants, UK and UAE into one form. It checks a project's country or geography field and treats a short list of US state names as the USA. It also removes a sector filter that only echoes the industry name, because that would hide every project.
sections.why: The code says the sector echo is removed because it would zero the match set, so this is deliberate.
sections.watch_out: The US state list is short and fixed in the code, so a US state not on the list will not match a USA filter.

sections.name: File setup (part 27)
sections.title: Keeping filter labels in sync
sections.what: Updates the match counts and chips on screen without rebuilding the input boxes, so the analyst's typing focus is not lost. It also converts the current filters into the form the server expects for slides, such as geography, technology, outcome and project names.
sections.why: The code says matched project names are always sent so slide generation respects the filter.
sections.watch_out: Project names are sent only when there are 400 or fewer matches. With more, they are dropped without a message, and the server may use a looser filter.

sections.name: File setup (part 28)
sections.title: Reading the filter box into filters
sections.what: Reads the text in the filter prompt box, runs the simple text parser, and stores the result as the current filters, noting where they came from. It also prepares a list of countries and a sample of up to 24 projects to send to the server for a smarter reading.
sections.why: The code shows the intent to parse locally first and call the server only when needed.
sections.watch_out: Only the first 24 projects are sent as examples, so the server's reading is based on a partial sample of the industry.

sections.name: File setup (part 29)
sections.title: Asking the server to read filters
sections.what: When the simple parse finds no matches, sends the request to the server for an AI-based reading and applies the filters it returns. If that still gives zero matches, it records a lesson on the server and makes a local repaired version by dropping the sector and search text. It needs a signed-in token and shows notices along the way.
sections.why: Likely reason: the AI reading handles phrasing the simple parse misses, and recorded lessons help later requests. The code describes the local repair as matching the server's lessons.
sections.watch_out: Without a sign-in token the AI reading does not run, and the page falls back to the simple parse, so results can differ between signed-in and signed-out users.

sections.name: File setup (part 30)
sections.title: Peer-set fingerprint and confirmation state
sections.what: Finishes the notice about the filter reading, then builds a text fingerprint from the industry and all filter values. It clears any confirmed peer set when the fingerprint changes, and returns the confirmed projects only while the fingerprint still matches. It also starts building the confirmation panel that lists keep, drop and uncertain verdicts.
sections.why: Likely reason: stops a confirmed peer set from quietly surviving after the analyst changes a filter.
sections.watch_out: The fingerprint is compared in lower case, and it includes the prompt text, so any edit to the prompt makes an accepted peer set stale and asks for confirmation again.

sections.name: File setup (part 31)
sections.title: Starting peer-set research
sections.what: Shows the rest of the confirmation panel's buttons: accept the recommended set, keep all Yard matches, or cancel. It also starts research by freezing the current Yard matches, showing a loading state where every project is marked keep for now, and reporting the research as pending.
sections.why: The code says the Yard count is frozen while research runs, so the number does not change under the analyst.
sections.watch_out: Accept buttons are disabled while loading, which prevents accepting placeholder verdicts. Research needs a signed-in token, and zero matches stop it with a notice.

sections.name: File setup (part 32)
sections.title: Calling the peer-set research service
sections.what: Sends the frozen project list and filter settings to the server's confirm-filter service, which checks each project's geography using AI and web research. On success it stores the keep, drop and uncertain lists and a summary. On failure it lets the analyst keep the Yard count or cancel.
sections.why: Likely reason: the fallback lets the analyst keep working when research fails. The code also states a research cap, maxResearch.
sections.watch_out: Research is capped at 8 projects. How the rest are judged is not visible in this code, so the recommended count may not cover every project.

sections.name: File setup (part 33)
sections.title: Accepting the peer set and building the prompt
sections.what: Finishes the error path, then lets the analyst accept either the recommended set or all Yard matches. The accepted set becomes the deck's selection. It also builds the text sent to generation, including the filter request and the standard template name.
sections.why: The code says the accepted set becomes the deck selection so generation uses the same projects the analyst saw.
sections.watch_out: If research kept no projects but Yard had matches, accepting quietly falls back to all Yard matches, which may be more than the analyst expected.

sections.name: File setup (part 34)
sections.title: Notices, view buttons and deck toggle
sections.what: Shows short notices that fade after about two seconds. Builds the view switch: the deck shows only the PPTX option, while industry and project pages also offer HTML. It also builds the add-to-deck button and a helper that makes initials from a name.
sections.why: The code limits the deck view to PPTX output for analysts.
sections.watch_out: Notices disappear after about two seconds, so an important message can be missed. The methodology option is never shown in this view.

sections.name: File setup (part 35)
sections.title: Sidebar highlight, home cards and industry page start
sections.what: Highlights the chosen role in the sidebar, then builds the home page's stats and industry cards, or a message when no industry data is loaded. It also starts the industry page, with its breadcrumb trail, title and tagline, and a switch between HTML and PPTX views.
sections.why: The message depends on whether the Yard data has loaded, so the analyst sees loading or empty states rather than a blank page.
sections.watch_out: The industry page and home cards use the DOTS color table, which is empty in the code shown, so color dots may appear blank.

sections.name: File setup (part 36)
sections.title: Industry page layout and company list
sections.what: Builds the main part of an industry page. It shows either a summary view or a grid of project cards, with a friendly message when a filter hides every project, and adds a side panel listing the companies in that industry. It also defines `chipEl`, a small filter button.
sections.why: Likely reason: the whole page is assembled as one block of HTML text and then placed on screen at once.
sections.watch_out: The empty-results message appears only in the project grid view, so the summary view never shows it.

sections.name: File setup (part 37)
sections.title: Project page header and helper summaries
sections.what: Defines three helpers, `derivedTimeline`, `derivedStakeholders` and `derivedLessons`, that build the timeline, stakeholder list and lessons for a project from whatever data is available. Then `renderProject` starts the top bar with breadcrumbs, the project name, status tag, and an add-to-deck button, and switches to the slide editor when the deck view is selected.
sections.why: Likely reason: project records can be incomplete, so the helpers build fallback content so the page still shows something useful.
sections.watch_out: When a project has no dates, the timeline falls back to a single status line, which can look like a complete timeline.

sections.name: File setup (part 38)
sections.title: Project page body and related projects
sections.what: Fills in the project page body with an overview, lesson blocks, a delivery timeline, an at-a-glance fact panel, stakeholder links and a list of related projects. Related projects match on owner, process route or country, and the list falls back to any other projects in the same industry when nothing matches.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the layout itself: the page is split into a main column and a side column.
sections.watch_out: When no project matches on owner, route or country, the 'Related' list shows unrelated projects from the same industry, which can mislead a reader.

sections.name: File setup (part 39)
sections.title: Company page totals and layout
sections.what: `companyStats` adds up planned capital for a company's projects, falling back to actual capital when planned is missing, and counts on-track and delayed projects. `renderCompany` then draws the company page with four headline numbers, an overview paragraph and project cards.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but the totals give a quick portfolio picture for each company on one page.
sections.watch_out: Projects with no capital figure add nothing to the total, and the 'delayed' count also includes over-budget projects, so the numbers can be understated or blended.

sections.name: File setup (part 40)
sections.title: Outcome labels and deck spine
sections.what: `outcomeOf` labels each project as Overran, Cautionary, Delivered or In progress using its status and end date text. `buildRecipeStyleSlides` then starts building a deck from projects that carry fact records, creating a cover, an executive summary, an agenda and a framework overview.
sections.why: Likely reason: the deck's themes come from the evidence in the records, not from a fixed template, as the comments say.
sections.watch_out: The Delivered label depends on the words in the end date field matching a pattern, so unusual wording can change a project's label without any warning.

sections.name: File setup (part 41)
sections.title: Evidence slides and assessment slide
sections.what: `buildRecipeStyleSlides` creates one slide per theme, listing up to five evidence lines and up to three source links. It then adds an assessment slide that summarises the first three themes and first three projects. Last, `recipeApiSlidesToBeacon` begins converting slides returned by the analysis service into this page's format.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but the assessment slide gives the reader a closing summary tied to the evidence.
sections.watch_out: Project names are shortened at the first opening bracket, so two projects with similar names may look identical on the slide.

sections.name: File setup (part 42)
sections.title: Converting service slides and choosing the source
sections.what: `recipeApiSlidesToBeacon` finishes converting slides from the analysis service. It fills in evidence lines for theme slides that lack them and gives each slide a section label. `activeRecipeSlides` then uses those service slides when present and otherwise uses the local fallback.
sections.why: The code comment says the official preview must come from the analysis service, not from local placeholders.
sections.watch_out: A theme slide that has no title can cause an error here, because the code reads the title text directly.

sections.name: File setup (part 43)
sections.title: Placeholder slides and slide drawing start
sections.what: `slidesForIndustry`, `slidesForProject` and `slidesForDeck` supply simple placeholder slides for the industry, project and deck views when no analysis is loaded. `slideHTML` then starts choosing a drawing style for each slide kind, handling cover, center note, agenda, executive summary and overview slides.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page should still show something useful before the analysis has run.
sections.watch_out: `slidesForProject` reads the industry name directly, so a project whose industry is missing from the list will cause an error.

sections.name: File setup (part 44)
sections.title: Overview and pillar slide layouts
sections.what: Draws overview slides as columns of lettered items and pillar slides as a coloured banner with a principle box, good and weak signal notes, and up to four columns of evidence bullets. It also starts the table layout used for directory and data sheet slides.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but the layout follows the house style the slides are meant to match.
sections.watch_out: The pillar number shown in the banner is read from digits in the title, so a title without digits always shows the first number.

sections.name: File setup (part 45)
sections.title: Table, chart and findings slide layouts
sections.what: Draws directory and data sheet tables, scoring criteria, geography columns, bar charts, a coloured scorecard grid and a findings list. Each one turns the stored slide data into positioned HTML.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but each layout matches one kind of slide the analysis can produce.
sections.watch_out: Bar heights have a minimum of eight pixels, so a bar for zero still appears as a small block and can suggest a value that is not there.

sections.name: File setup (part 46)
sections.title: Bubble chart, case profiles and fallback layout
sections.what: Finishes the findings list, then draws a bubble chart of cost overrun against schedule overrun, with at most forty points. It also draws case profile slides with key facts and a pillar-by-pillar assessment, a simple scorecard table, and a generic bullet layout for any other slide kind.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but case profiles show one project's story next to the themes.
sections.watch_out: If many projects share the same values, their bubbles overlap and only a limited number of points are drawn, so the chart may hide some projects.

sections.name: File setup (part 47)
sections.title: Generic bullets and deck editor layout
sections.what: Draws the default bullet list, with extra lines inside a bullet shown in smaller grey text, and wraps each slide in a frame. `renderDeckEditor` then builds the editor with a thumbnail strip, a large preview and buttons for generating the analysis or downloading the PowerPoint file.
sections.why: Likely reason: the editor is simplified for non-admin users, showing only slides and hiding the admin tools.
sections.watch_out: Non-admin users see a leaner screen with fewer buttons, so a missing button is by design and not a fault.

sections.name: File setup (part 48)
sections.title: Turning analysis results into slides
sections.what: `slidesFromCanonical` turns the finished analysis result into slide objects: cover, executive summary, agenda, an overview with columns, and one slide per pillar with lettered sub-points and evidence. The comments say the output should match a reference layout.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the comment about matching the reference layout.
sections.watch_out: The cover title falls back to a fixed sentence when the analysis does not supply one, so a generic title can appear on a real deck.

sections.name: File setup (part 49)
sections.title: Project groups, directory and geography
sections.what: Fills pillar evidence lines from backing facts when the analysis lacks analysis text. It then groups projects into Delivered, Overran or Cautionary, and In progress groups, builds a directory table, and groups projects by region for a geography slide.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but the groups give the reader a quick split of outcomes.
sections.watch_out: The directory shows only the first nine rows of up to thirty-six, and any outcome label that is not recognised is quietly placed under In progress.

sections.name: File setup (part 50)
sections.title: Geography, scorecard grid and bubble data
sections.what: Adds the geography slide, then a scorecard grid marking each pillar for up to eighteen projects as strong, mixed, risk or not applicable. The bubble chart data uses placeholder positions for projects that lack overrun figures, based on their outcome label.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but the grid lets readers compare projects across pillars at a glance.
sections.watch_out: The placeholder positions for missing overrun figures are rule-based guesses, not measured values, yet they appear on the chart as if they were real data.

sections.name: File setup (part 51)
sections.title: Case profiles, appendix and text trimming
sections.what: Builds key facts and pillar takeaways for up to ten projects, skipping any project with neither. It adds an appendix of up to eight fact entries and closing slides from extra text supplied by the analysis, applies theme colours, and cuts long text to a set length. The section also starts `loadAgentCanonical`, which fetches the saved analysis result for a run.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but case profiles and the appendix give supporting detail behind the summary slides.
sections.watch_out: Projects with no facts or takeaways are dropped without any message, so the reader may not notice missing cases.

sections.name: File setup (part 52)
sections.title: Loading results and PowerPoint setup
sections.what: `loadAgentCanonical` fetches the saved analysis result for a run and keeps a copy for later comparison. `ensureFreshPptx` asks the server to build a new PowerPoint file from the current theme settings and then reloads the slides. The section also sets the slide size and colour scheme used when reading PowerPoint files.
sections.why: Likely reason: the saved result must be loaded before any slide or file can be built from it.
sections.watch_out: `loadAgentCanonical` returns nothing on any error and shows no message, so a failed load looks the same as no result.

sections.name: File setup (part 53)
sections.title: Reading PowerPoint shapes and colours
sections.what: Functions such as `parseV2ShapeBlock` and `parseV2SlideXml` read the inner XML of a PowerPoint slide to find shape positions, sizes, text, fonts, bold text, colours and the background. This lets the page show a preview of the downloaded file without running PowerPoint.
sections.why: Likely reason: showing a preview in the browser is simpler than sending the file to a server for rendering.
sections.watch_out: The code uses pattern matching on XML text rather than a full XML reader, so unusual files may be misread.

sections.name: File setup (part 54)
sections.title: Unpacking PowerPoint and drawing preview frames
sections.what: `loadV2SlideModels` opens the PowerPoint file as a zip archive, reads the slide size, and parses each slide in number order. `renderV2SlideFrame` then draws each slide as positioned boxes and text that resemble the original.
sections.why: Likely reason: a PowerPoint file is a zip archive of XML, so the browser can read it directly once a zip library is loaded.
sections.watch_out: Slides are ordered by the numbers in their file names, and a text size floor makes small text appear larger than it would in PowerPoint.

sections.name: File setup (part 55)
sections.title: Thumbnail strip and page counter
sections.what: `renderV2ThumbStrip` draws the row of small slide thumbnails. `indicationPreviewHTML` builds the preview toolbar with previous and next buttons, a page counter, and a label showing whether the deck is filled or still a template. `syncV2PreviewPageLabel` and `syncV2ThumbSelection` keep the counter and highlighted thumbnail in step with the current slide.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, but thumbnails let the reader jump around the deck quickly.
sections.watch_out: The label says the preview is the same file as the download, so the preview can only be trusted if the stored file has been kept up to date.

sections.name: File setup (part 56)
sections.title: Showing and paging through preview slides
sections.what: `paintV2PreviewSlide` redraws the current slide, updates the page counter, and rebuilds the thumbnails if the count has changed. `mountIndicationPreview` loads the stored PowerPoint file for the first time, while `stepV2Preview` and `goV2PreviewSlide` handle next, previous and jump-to-slide.
sections.why: Likely reason: the token counter in `mountIndicationPreview` stops an older, slower load from overwriting a newer one when the user acts quickly.
sections.watch_out: The token counter must be kept in any change, or a slow old preview can replace the slide the user is looking at.

sections.name: File setup (part 57)
sections.title: Opening preview and downloading the deck
sections.what: `viewIndicationPptx` shows the filled deck in the page, restoring the last completed analysis file when one exists. `openIndicationDeck` downloads the file, naming it with the run id when it is filled, or with the template name otherwise.
sections.why: Likely reason: the file is restored from a saved run so that reopening the page does not lose the filled deck.
sections.watch_out: If no completed run can be restored, `viewIndicationPptx` quietly loads the blank template, so the user may preview or download an empty deck with only a short notice.

sections.name: File setup (part 58)
sections.title: Download errors and building fill values
sections.what: `openIndicationDeck` shows any download error as a short message. `xmlEscape` protects special characters before text is placed in the PowerPoint file. `buildV2FillMap` starts building the text values that fill the template, such as the deck title, date, thesis and project counts, based on the current selection.
sections.why: Likely reason: the template is filled by swapping placeholder text, so the values must be safe to place in XML.
sections.watch_out: The fill step matches the template's placeholder wording exactly, so editing the template text will stop values from being filled in.

sections.name: File setup (part 59)
sections.title: Template text replacement and library loading
sections.what: `buildV2FillMap` finishes by storing extra values such as project names, segments and the first twelve projects' details. `replaceXmlText` and `replaceFirstXmlText` swap placeholder text in the PowerPoint XML, and `ensureJSZip` loads the zip library from a local file when it is first needed.
sections.why: Likely reason: the template's placeholders are changed directly in the file so the original styling is kept.
sections.watch_out: Placeholder text split across several pieces inside the file may not match, so it stays unfilled without any warning.

sections.name: File setup (part 60)
sections.title: Fills the indication template in the browser
sections.what: Loads the standard PowerPoint template, copies project names, segments and values into each slide's placeholder text, and keeps the finished file in memory for the preview. The code comment says this runs on the client with no server writes.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the deck be filled in the browser without saving anything on the server.
sections.watch_out: Filling works by matching exact placeholder text, so any wording change in the template silently stops values from being filled.

sections.name: File setup (part 61)
sections.title: Downloads the latest generated PowerPoint
sections.what: When the user clicks Download PPTX, fetches the finished deck from the agent service, or opens the filled template when no agent is used, and saves it as a file. The file is named recipe_for_success.pptx for the harness output and recipe.pptx otherwise.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code. It appears to give the user a file that matches what the preview shows.
sections.watch_out: The download re-fetches a specific generation tag so the file matches the preview, so changing that tag logic can make the download differ from the preview.

sections.name: File setup (part 62)
sections.title: Loads slide list from the agent service
sections.what: Asks the agent service for the slide list using the chosen theme colours and font, converts each slide into the app's format, and redraws the preview. It returns nothing and shows no message if the request fails.
sections.why: Likely reason: the server holds the real slide content, and the browser only displays it.
sections.watch_out: Errors are swallowed silently, so a failed load looks like nothing happened.

sections.name: File setup (part 63)
sections.title: Builds the preview from typed inputs
sections.what: Layers the chosen industry, the user's filter prompt and the project count onto the stored deck outline so the preview updates as the user types. Before any run exists, it builds a draft deck with five placeholder pillars.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the user see an approximate deck before the server has produced anything.
sections.watch_out: The default industry differs between two functions, and the default count of 136 is fixed in code, so changing one place without the other gives inconsistent previews.

sections.name: File setup (part 64)
sections.title: Chat commands edit the preview
sections.what: Reads simple chat messages such as rename a pillar, set the thesis, add a centre slide, or show or hide the run ID, and applies them to a copy of the deck outline. Any longer message of more than 24 characters becomes the new thesis.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fallback that mirrors the server's chat commands when the free-form assistant is unavailable, as the comment says.
sections.watch_out: Any long sentence typed into chat silently replaces the thesis, so a stray message can overwrite earlier work.

sections.name: File setup (part 65)
sections.title: Refreshes the preview while typing
sections.what: Re-applies the filter prompt and chat text to the slides already on screen. The cover subtitle, first executive bullet, pillar names and thesis update without waiting for the server.
sections.why: Likely reason: avoids a server round trip on every keystroke.
sections.watch_out: Pillar renames are matched by position, which assumes the pillar IDs P1, P2 and so on line up with the column order.

sections.name: File setup (part 66)
sections.title: Redraws the deck strip and main slide
sections.what: Finishes the live update, which can hide the run ID on the cover or add a centre note slide. It then repaints the thumbnail strip and the large slide, and labels the strip as live or draft.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps the on-screen deck in step with what the user has typed.
sections.watch_out: Nothing is painted unless the deck page is open in the PPTX view, so changes made elsewhere only appear after returning to that view.

sections.name: File setup (part 67)
sections.title: Delays updates and draws the chat panel
sections.what: Waits 180 milliseconds after the last keystroke before refreshing, switches to the PPTX view if needed, and builds the assistant panel with its message log and suggestion buttons. The suggestions and placeholder text change depending on whether a run exists and whether free-form chat is enabled.
sections.why: Likely reason: the short wait stops the preview from redrawing on every letter typed.
sections.watch_out: The free-form chat flag comes from the agent's capabilities, so if that flag is missing the panel silently falls back to stub commands.

sections.name: File setup (part 68)
sections.title: Deck page top bar and controls
sections.what: Builds the Deck Builder heading and its buttons: Generate Recipe, Resume, View PPTX and Download PPTX. It then adds the status area for analysts or the run panel for admins, and shows any halt message.
sections.why: The comment says the analyst view is PPTX-first, and the code forces analysts into that view.
sections.watch_out: Resume is greyed out unless the harness is marked resumable and no recipe is running, so after a crash it may stay disabled until that flag is set.

sections.name: File setup (part 69)
sections.title: Keeps the deck visible during generation
sections.what: In PPTX mode, shows a waiting panel while a run is in progress, restores the last finished deck when the user returns to the page, and otherwise shows the empty template state.
sections.why: The code comments say the page must never go blank during generation and must not start a second generation.
sections.watch_out: Restoring the deck depends on a saved run ID in browser storage, so if that ID is cleared the page falls back to the empty state.

sections.name: File setup (part 70)
sections.title: Methodology view and source project list
sections.what: Shows the methodology page to admins only, and to others shows either the recipe iframe or the list of source projects grouped by industry with selection counts. The empty-deck message is on a line that is cut off in the source given here, so its exact wording is not visible.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The methodology branch depends on the deck view being set to methodology, which analysts cannot choose.

sections.name: File setup (part 71)
sections.title: Project checkboxes, reading view and expert cards
sections.what: Draws each project as a checkbox row showing location and status, builds a read-only lesson summary grouped by industry, and defines a card layout for experts.
sections.why: Reason not stated for the expert card. The experts page in this section does not call it, so it may be left over from an earlier design.
sections.watch_out: The reading view assumes every selected project ID exists in the project list, so a missing ID will cause an error.

sections.name: File setup (part 72)
sections.title: Switching between pages
sections.what: Shows the chosen page, scrolls it to the top, remembers the last Home or Deck page in browser storage, and redraws that page. Choosing admin silently switches the role to analyst and opens the deck page instead.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets the app return the user to where they last were.
sections.watch_out: Any request for the admin page is quietly redirected, so someone looking for admin tools will land on the deck instead.

sections.name: File setup (part 73)
sections.title: Admin lock removed and run stage labels
sections.what: Keeps the admin unlock functions, but they now show a message and keep the user as analyst. Also defines the list of internal run stages and the simpler labels shown to users.
sections.why: The code comment says the admin view was removed in Volume 2 and analysts only.
sections.watch_out: Browser session flags for admin are still read and cleared, so they may be stale even though the admin view no longer exists.

sections.name: File setup (part 74)
sections.title: Plain messages for failed runs
sections.what: Turns internal stage names and error text into short sentences, such as asking the user to loosen filters when no projects match. Also builds the Pristine or Smoke badge that shows how a run was produced.
sections.why: Likely reason: keeps technical detail away from analysts while still telling them what to do.
sections.watch_out: Messages are chosen by matching words in the error text, so rewording an internal error can cause a wrong or generic message to appear.

sections.name: File setup (part 75)
sections.title: Top status bar for analysts
sections.what: Shows one status line that reads as generating, deck ready, failed or interrupted, with chart warnings where relevant. When done, it adds Open PPTX and Promote / Improve buttons.
sections.why: Likely reason: gives analysts one simple status instead of the full admin panel.
sections.watch_out: The chart warning thresholds, such as 40 percent insufficient data and fewer than 3 plotted points, are fixed in code, so they may not match the server's own rules.

sections.name: File setup (part 76)
sections.title: Promote wording dialog and admin status
sections.what: Builds the Promote changes dialog, where a user edits one statement and saves it as a lesson for the next run. The on-screen text says the lesson goes to recipe_harness, not POPPY. Also builds the admin status pill.
sections.why: The dialog text itself explains that the lesson is saved for the next run.
sections.watch_out: The save target is named only in this wording, so anyone changing where lessons are stored must also update this text.

sections.name: File setup (part 77)
sections.title: Override panel for halted runs
sections.what: When a run stops on failed checks, lists those checks with a red or amber severity label. The analyst ticks the faults they accept, confirms with a checkbox, gives a reason, and then continues the run.
sections.why: The on-screen text explains that waivers are kept visible and that the run continues through the later stages.
sections.watch_out: Critical severity is decided by three hard-coded check names, so renaming one of those checks changes how it is labelled.

sections.name: File setup (part 78)
sections.title: Progress steps and quality coach
sections.what: Shows a status pill, the mode badge, and a five-step progress track with the current step highlighted. Below it shows the quality coach's headline, suggestions and research targets.
sections.why: Likely reason: shows progress as plain steps that an analyst can follow.
sections.watch_out: The progress track finds its position from the stage name, so a stage missing from the list shows the generic label Working.

sections.name: File setup (part 79)
sections.title: English enhancer status and filter bar
sections.what: Shows whether the AI writing layer is ready, is using a fallback, or is pending, with a Re-Enhance English button. Also builds the filter row with industry, count, filter text, Apply Filter, the framework option and Generate Recipe.
sections.why: The code comment says the enhancer is the LLM analysis layer that writes thesis and narratives.
sections.watch_out: The match count only shows the confirmed number when the filter fingerprint still matches, so editing the filter text without confirming can leave a stale count on screen.

sections.name: File setup (part 80)
sections.title: Admin download buttons and review prompt
sections.what: Builds an admin-only row of buttons for the HTML, methodology and PPTX outputs. The review prompt appears as soon as any output exists and offers a button to open Human Review, or to unlock admin if it is locked.
sections.why: The code comment says feedback opens before the LLM grader finishes, which is intended.
sections.watch_out: The Open Human Review button routes to the admin page, which the earlier section shows is redirected to the deck, so this button may not reach a review screen.

sections.name: File setup (part 81)
sections.title: Run state banner and grader card start
sections.what: The admin banner shows the run status and a chip for each stage. The grader card shows the quality coach's suggestions and research targets, and starts the table of scores.
sections.why: The comment says the banner is the admin-only full state track.
sections.watch_out: The grader card shows a waiting message until grader data arrives, so an empty card does not mean the grading failed.

sections.name: File setup (part 82)
sections.title: Grader scores and human review form
sections.what: Builds the score table with pass, warn or fail labels, the corrections list, and a note on the AI coach showing whether it was skipped, failed or worked. Also builds the Human Review box where an admin types findings, saves them, and approves the latest draft.
sections.why: The on-screen text says approved phrases are written back to the gate and rubric files.
sections.watch_out: Approving changes stored gate and rubric files, as the screen says, so an approval affects future runs and not just this one.

sections.name: File setup (part 83)
sections.title: Timing and golden benchmark tables
sections.what: Shows two admin tables. The efficiency table compares expected and actual time for each stage and flags slow ones. The golden table shows how far the run's numbers are from a reference run. Token and cost figures are stated as not yet available.
sections.why: The on-screen text says LLM research cost tracking is not wired up yet.
sections.watch_out: Cost is shown as a note rather than a number, so no cost figure should be expected until that tracking is added.

sections.name: File setup (part 84)
sections.title: Saved checkpoints table for admins
sections.what: Lists each run stage with whether it was reached, when, a short file name, and a summary of recipe lines and analysis. The table is built from saved checkpoints so an interrupted run can be resumed.
sections.why: The on-screen text says each reached stage stores its content so a crashed run can resume.
sections.watch_out: The file name is taken by splitting a stored path on slashes, so unusual path formats can show a wrong or empty name.

sections.name: File setup (part 85)
sections.title: Admin card showing harness test results
sections.what: Builds the POPPY harness panel on the admin page. It shows the run mode, whether the run counts as pristine, any fallback, a table of pass or fail checks from E0 to E9, a count of regressions against earlier memory, and the stages the run went through.
sections.why: Likely reason: the admin needs a quick view of whether the automated pipeline run passed its quality checks.
sections.watch_out: Check details are cut to 160 characters, so a long failure message can look shorter than it really is.

sections.name: File setup (part 86)
sections.title: Builds the whole admin page
sections.what: Assembles the admin page from its parts. If admin is not unlocked it shows a locked message instead. Otherwise it draws the top bar, progress, artifacts, the harness panel, gate cards A to D (D appears only once used), efficiency and grader cards, the review card, and a run log of events.
sections.why: Likely reason: one function puts the page together in a fixed order so the admin sees status before the details.
sections.watch_out: The Resume button is enabled only when the run status is HALTED, so other states cannot be resumed from this button.

sections.name: File setup (part 87)
sections.title: Artifact download links and the auth switch
sections.what: Creates download links for each finished output (HTML, canonical data, methodology PDF, PPTX, manuscript, verification, relevance) and an analysis link, but only for outputs that exist. It also holds the global switch that turns off sign-in checks and the helper that builds the recipe scope from the chosen industries and deck projects.
sections.why: Likely reason: links appear only when outputs exist so people do not click dead links. The auth switch is marked TEMPORARY in the code.
sections.watch_out: AUTH_DISABLED is currently true, so authToken returns a fixed placeholder and sign-in checks are skipped; this must be reverted before real use.

sections.name: File setup (part 88)
sections.title: Choosing which projects go into a recipe
sections.what: Decides which projects are sent when a recipe is built. It uses any confirmed peer set first, then projects picked in the deck, then active filters, and finally the whole industry. In not-all mode it limits the list to between 1 and 500 projects. It also builds the request body, which includes flags for requiring agents and regenerating the framework, and copies the recipe slides and pillar names into the preview.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond comments that explain the priority order.
sections.watch_out: An empty project list means the whole industry is sent, so a forgotten filter can make a much larger run than intended.

sections.name: File setup (part 89)
sections.title: Loading a recipe preview from the server
sections.what: Asks the server for a preview of the recipe using the current deck projects, then copies its slides and pillars into the preview and adds a chat message naming the pillars. If no one is signed in or the deck is empty, it shows a message and stops.
sections.why: Likely reason: the preview is built on the server so it matches the final deck logic instead of inventing its own pillars.
sections.watch_out: Errors appear only as a short pop-up, so a failed preview leaves the old view in place without a clear explanation.

sections.name: File setup (part 90)
sections.title: Filling in output links after a run
sections.what: After a run finishes, fills in the web addresses for the HTML, methodology, PPTX and canonical data so the viewers and downloads work. If the run is halted it fetches the override information instead. Errors are swallowed and nothing is returned.
sections.why: Likely reason: outputs are wired in one place so every screen refresh uses the same addresses.
sections.watch_out: The PDF and PPTX addresses end in a timestamp that changes on every call, so the browser will reload them rather than use a cached copy.

sections.name: File setup (part 91)
sections.title: Submitting analyst waivers to continue a halted run
sections.what: Lets an analyst waive chosen failed checks on a halted run. It requires a tick in the acknowledgment box, a reason of at least 10 characters, and at least one selected check. It then saves the waivers as feedback, shows a message, and waits for the run to continue.
sections.why: Likely reason: a halted run should continue only when a person accepts the specific faults, and the reason is kept on record.
sections.watch_out: The actor name is fixed to 'Beacon analyst', so the record does not show which real person approved the waiver.

sections.name: File setup (part 92)
sections.title: Watching a continued run until it stops
sections.what: After waivers are submitted, checks the run once a second for up to 300 seconds. It refreshes the screen and stops with a halt message if the run halts again or a success message if it completes. If the run is still going after that, it reports that Refresh must be used.
sections.why: Likely reason: a fixed wait limit stops the page from polling forever.
sections.watch_out: Runs that take longer than about five minutes show a still-running error even though the server keeps working.

sections.name: File setup (part 93)
sections.title: Background progress checks for the deck run
sections.what: Holds helpers for the deck run. One checks whether a finished PPTX is loaded. Another starts a timer that asks the server for progress every 2.5 seconds, updates the status line, loads the deck when done, and prompts for Resume if the run fails or is interrupted.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page cannot hold a long request open, so it checks progress on a timer.
sections.watch_out: The timer stops only when the run succeeds, fails or is interrupted, so a run stuck in another state keeps polling.

sections.name: File setup (part 94)
sections.title: Remembering and reading the saved harness run
sections.what: Finds the saved run ID from browser storage or current memory. It then asks the server for that run's status and sets whether the run can be resumed. A run that already succeeded also gets its PPTX address stored.
sections.why: Likely reason: the saved ID lets the deck come back after a page reload.
sections.watch_out: If the server cannot be reached, the run is marked resumable whenever an ID exists, even if the server would refuse to resume it.

sections.name: File setup (part 95)
sections.title: Reloading a finished deck after navigation
sections.what: If a run has succeeded, downloads its PPTX again so the deck viewer is not blank when the user returns to the page. It prefers the saved address and marks the preview as visible. It does nothing while a run is busy.
sections.why: Likely reason: the deck is held only in browser memory, so it must be fetched again after navigating.
sections.watch_out: A failed download is only logged to the console, so the user sees a blank viewer with no message.

sections.name: File setup (part 96)
sections.title: Waiting for a harness run to finish
sections.what: Polls the server every 2 seconds for up to about 6 minutes. It announces each change of phase, throws a visible error if the run fails or is interrupted, and throws an error when time runs out while the run is still not complete.
sections.why: Likely reason: the time limit prevents the page waiting forever on a run that never finishes.
sections.watch_out: A legitimate run longer than about 6 minutes reports an error even though it may still complete on the server.

sections.name: File setup (part 97)
sections.title: Saving a manual text change to a run
sections.what: Sends a revised piece of text to the server for a chosen field, by default the first insight headline, with a note. The change is marked for automatic approval. The same section also loads the PPTX file into memory for the deck viewer.
sections.why: Likely reason: lets an analyst fix wording without rerunning the whole pipeline.
sections.watch_out: The change is auto-approved, so it is applied without a second review step.

sections.name: File setup (part 98)
sections.title: Resuming an interrupted deck run
sections.what: Asks the server to resume a saved run. If it was already complete, it loads the existing deck. Otherwise it waits for completion, loads the PPTX, and adds a chat message with the quality tier and model run count. In every case it clears the busy flag and refreshes the status.
sections.why: Likely reason: a resume continues from saved checkpoints so earlier work is not repeated.
sections.watch_out: The busy flag is cleared in a final step that always runs, so an error in the middle does not leave the page stuck on busy.

sections.name: File setup (part 99)
sections.title: Start of the Generate Recipe button
sections.what: Runs when the user presses Generate Recipe. It first reattaches to a run already in progress rather than starting a duplicate. It asks for confirmation before replacing a filled deck. It then reads the industry and selection settings, and stops with a message if the filters match no projects or no industry is picked.
sections.why: Likely reason: this prevents duplicate runs and avoids replacing a deck by accident.
sections.watch_out: The overwrite prompt is a browser confirm box; cancelling it restores the old deck rather than generating a new one.

sections.name: File setup (part 100)
sections.title: Checks before a recipe run starts
sections.what: Requires that an analyst has confirmed the peer set whenever filters are active, and asks for research if not. Then it marks the screen busy, clears the old recipe, and starts either the server harness run or a simpler fill done inside the browser.
sections.why: Likely reason: confirmation keeps the peer-set size stable so counts do not shift between runs.
sections.watch_out: The confirmation is tied to a fingerprint of the filters, so any filter change requires confirming again.

sections.name: File setup (part 101)
sections.title: Starting and watching the harness run
sections.what: Sends the recipe request to the harness start endpoint, stores the returned run ID, starts progress checks, waits for completion, loads the PPTX, and adds a chat message with the tier and model run count.
sections.why: Likely reason: the work runs on the server, so the page starts it and then watches it.
sections.watch_out: If the server accepts the request but returns no run ID, the function fails and the run cannot be tracked from this page.

sections.name: File setup (part 102)
sections.title: Test helpers for empty and resume runs
sections.what: agentStartEmptyGateB creates a test run with a filter that matches nothing, to check that the Gate B failure appears, then reports the halt reason. agentResume asks the server to resume the current run and waits up to about 30 seconds for it to succeed or halt.
sections.why: Likely reason: these are testing and admin helpers for the pipeline gates.
sections.watch_out: The resume wait stops after about 30 seconds, so a longer run can look unfinished even though it is still working.

sections.name: File setup (part 103)
sections.title: Refresh, deck view, and start of click handling
sections.what: agentRefresh reloads output links for the current run and redraws the admin and deck pages. presentPptx switches to the deck page in PPTX view. This section also starts the main click handler, which routes harness resume, the indication PPTX view, and the Improve panel open, close and save buttons.
sections.why: Likely reason: refreshing without restarting the run lets the user see the latest output.
sections.watch_out: agentRefresh does nothing useful and only shows a message when there is no current run.

sections.name: File setup (part 104)
sections.title: Main click handler: slides, themes and override
sections.what: Continues the main click handler. It routes slide step and jump buttons, applies colour themes, downloads a fresh PPTX, runs the analyst override, and re-analyzes English.
sections.why: Likely reason: one central click listener means buttons do not each need their own listener.
sections.watch_out: The theme save to the server ignores errors, so a failed save can still look successful to the user.

sections.name: File setup (part 105)
sections.title: Click actions for filters and deck chat
sections.what: Continues the click handler for the natural language filter (apply, confirm, keep the Yard list, cancel), clearing deck filters, selecting every filtered project, and sending a message from the deck chat box.
sections.why: Likely reason: these buttons all change which projects are in the peer set, so they are grouped together.
sections.watch_out: Select-filtered toggles every visible project at once, so one click can remove projects the user meant to keep.

sections.name: File setup (part 106)
sections.title: Admin review: save findings and approve
sections.what: Saves a text note of review findings for the current run and sends it to the server. Approve sends a chosen draft finding to the server to be written back. Both actions need the admin password, read from session storage and sent in a request header.
sections.why: Likely reason: findings and approved changes are kept as feedback so later runs can learn from them.
sections.watch_out: Approve writes a change back to stored memory, so a mistaken click can affect future runs.

sections.name: File setup (part 107)
sections.title: Simple click actions for the rest of the page
sections.what: Handles many simpler buttons: toggling the side rail, switching role, locking admin, refreshing, running tests and recipes, navigating pages, opening industry, project and company pages, switching views and tabs, and cycling the status filter.
sections.why: Likely reason: one long chain of checks sends each button to its action.
sections.watch_out: The checks run in order and the first match wins, so reordering these lines can change which action a button triggers.

sections.name: File setup (part 108)
sections.title: Click actions for adding to the deck
sections.what: Handles adding and removing projects, industries and companies from the deck, opening and closing company lists, moving between slides, the add-slide button, the export button, chat suggestions, and the connect button.
sections.why: Likely reason: the deck is the shared selection that every recipe run uses.
sections.watch_out: The add-slide button only shows a message; it does not add a slide.

sections.name: File setup (part 109)
sections.title: Live typing and dropdown changes
sections.what: Reacts as the user types in the chat and filter boxes, changes the industry, toggles select all, and moves the project count control. Typing in the filter box waits about 180 milliseconds before re-reading the filters.
sections.why: Likely reason: waiting briefly avoids reloading the filter on every key press.
sections.watch_out: Typing in the filter box resets any filter confirmation, so the user must confirm again before generating.

sections.name: File setup (part 110)
sections.title: Chat: sends questions to the agent or a script
sections.what: Sends a chat message. If the run has a recipe, the message goes to the live agent, which may edit the deck and refresh the preview. If the run has no recipe, it shows a tip. With no run at all, it returns a canned reply from a fixed list.
sections.why: Likely reason: the canned fallback keeps the chat working when no live run exists.
sections.watch_out: The canned replies claim the deck was changed when nothing was edited, so they can mislead the user.

sections.name: File setup (part 111)
sections.title: Formatting money and turning Yard data into projects
sections.what: Turns Yard money values into short labels such as millions or thousands, adds up capital for a list of projects, works out a simple status for each project from its status text and delay, and maps raw Yard fields to the names the page uses.
sections.why: Likely reason: the page needs one consistent shape for projects regardless of the Yard source.
sections.watch_out: Status is inferred by matching words in the status text, and anything unmatched defaults to on-track.

sections.name: File setup (part 112)
sections.title: Grouping projects by owner and fetching Yard
sections.what: Finishes mapping each project. Groups projects by owner into company entries, capped at 60 owners, and builds segment counts for the top 8 technologies. Adds a helper that sends signed requests to Yard and treats an unauthorised reply as a sign-in problem.
sections.why: Likely reason: companies and segments power the industry pages without extra server calls.
sections.watch_out: Owners are grouped by exact name, so two spellings of the same operator show as separate companies.

sections.name: File setup (part 113)
sections.title: Loading every industry from Yard
sections.what: Loads each industry in turn from the Yard API, builds its stats, companies, segments and project lists, and stores them as the app's data. Once all are loaded it sets the home page totals, picks a starting industry, clears the deck, and writes a welcome chat message.
sections.why: Likely reason: loading all industries up front lets the rest of the page work from memory.
sections.watch_out: An industry that fails to load is only logged and skipped, so the page can look complete while missing data.

sections.name: File setup (part 114)
sections.title: Wiring the admin password box
sections.what: Connects the admin password dialog. Submitting checks the password, and a wrong one shows an error. Clicking outside the box or pressing Cancel closes it and returns to analyst view.
sections.why: Likely reason: a small wrapper keeps admin unlock separate from the rest of the page.
sections.watch_out: Cancel returns to the home page, while clicking outside stays on the current page, so the two exits behave differently.

sections.name: File setup (part 115)
sections.title: Starting the page and restoring the last state
sections.what: On load, sets the analyst view and shows the home page. If there is no sign-in, it sends the user to the login page after a short delay. Otherwise it loads Yard data, restores the last deck if one succeeded, reattaches to any run still in progress, and shows a status message.
sections.why: Likely reason: restoring state lets a user return to their deck after a reload.
sections.watch_out: The login redirect depends on the auth token, which the AUTH_DISABLED switch currently forces on, so the redirect is skipped in this build.

summary: A very large single-file prototype of the Lessons Learned Volume 2 page, which now sends visitors to a maintained tool. Only the first 506 of 5977 lines were visible.
purpose: Keeps old links to the prototype working and holds the page styles.
why: Stated in the code: the comment says old bookmarks now use the maintained native tool.
how: 1. Load the shared identity script. 2. Redirect the visitor to the lessons-learnt tool, keeping any query string. 3. Load the page styles, which define the layout, colors, and components. 4. The rest of the file, which was not visible, holds the page content and scripts.
inputs: The page address and its query string, the shared identity script, and Google Fonts.
outputs: A redirect to the maintained tool. If the redirect were removed, a styled prototype page.
risks: The redirect runs first, so visitors never see this page. The admin lock is only styling, so the real access check, which is not visible here, is what protects it.
debug: If old links fail, check that the lessons-learnt tool exists at the path the redirect names. If the page loops or shows nothing, check the redirect line first.
